html:
The Book of the Eparch is a Byzantine handbook of rules for the trade guilds of Constantinople, issued in the name of Emperor Leo VI around 911 or 912. The eparch was the city's governor, who judged its courts and oversaw its markets, prices and imports.

It names about twenty trades and sets out what each could and could not do:

  • notaries, bankers and money changers
  • silk merchants, silk dressers and makers of raw silk, whose purple cloth was closely controlled
  • dealers in linen, perfume, candles and soap
  • grocers, butchers, pork dealers, fishmongers, bakers and innkeepers

It fixed profit margins, controlled who could join a guild, barred members from moving into another trade, and limited what foreign merchants could buy and how long they could stay. Fines, flogging and shaving of the head backed the rules.

It is a key document for the economic history of the Byzantine Empire. It shows a state keeping tight control of the capital's food and of its most precious product, silk. Later privileges for Italian merchants, starting with the Golden Bull for Venice of 1082, loosened that control.
